verses.1: Al-Mizan distinguishes the truth of information from the truthfulness of its speaker. A report conforms to reality or not; separately, a speaker's words conform to his own belief or not. The hypocrites' testimony that Muhammad is God's Messenger is true in the first sense, and God confirms it, but they are liars in the second because their inward belief contradicts their outward testimony. That testimony implies the whole faith, including God's unity and the Day of Judgment. God's explicit confirmation clarifies that His final witness calls them liars for the informant's falsity, not because the reported Messengerhood is false.
verses.2: Al-Mizan explains that the hypocrites make their false oaths a shield. Sadd may mean that they turn themselves away from God's path, religion, or that, shielded by their oaths, they turn other people away by dissuasion, distortion, and corrupting resolve. Their deed is condemned as evil throughout the continuing course of their hypocrisy.
verses.3: Al-Mizan says the demonstrative may point to the preceding evil itself or to the whole record of lying, false oaths, turning from God's way, and harm. Believed then disbelieved can mean outwardly pronouncing the two testimonies while inwardly empty of faith; it may also include people who truly believed, then apostatized secretly and joined the hypocrites. In either case, their later disbelief includes mockery and rejection of rules. The sealed heart then cannot receive or follow truth, follows desire instead, and is thereby deprived of faith, understanding, hearing, and knowledge. This sealing, though attributed to God, is only retribution for their own deviation and never primary misguidance.
verses.4:
Al-Mizan generalizes the address beyond the Prophet: hypocrites impress observers by fine appearance and fluent, sweet speech. Inwardly they are like propped-up timber, lifeless, useless forms without understanding. Because they hide unbelief, they live in fearful estrangement and imagine every cry is against them. They are thus the especially dangerous enemy: hostile while counted as friends.

The imprecation may God fight them most plainly asks their killing, using fighting to intensify the adversity, though expulsion from mercy, a declarative damnation, and an exclamation of astonishment are reported alternatives. The context favors the imprecation. How are they turned back is surprise at their turning from truth, and may also function as rebuke rather than a real question.
verses.5: Al-Mizan says that when their treachery became apparent and hypocrites were invited to let the Messenger seek forgiveness for them, they turned their heads away. The idiom conveys tilting or averting the head in disdain, repulsion, and pride, while their visible withdrawal shows arrogance before the offer of forgiveness.
verses.6: Al-Mizan treats the equivalence of seeking forgiveness for hypocrites and not seeking it as a figure meaning that the desired benefit can never result. God's refusal to forgive is the answer to why the Prophet's prayer cannot help them. Forgiveness here would be guidance toward happiness and Paradise; their concealed disbelief and sealed hearts make them transgressors outside worship, and God does not guide transgressing people.
verses.7: Al-Mizan says the hypocrites urge others not to maintain the poor believers who remain close to the Messenger to aid him and enact his aims, hoping poverty will make them scatter and end his authority over them. God's ownership of the treasuries of heaven and earth rebuts them: His religion does not need their wealth and He can provide for whom He wills. He could enrich those believers, but poverty tests them and calls forth patience, worship, and obedience, leading to noble reward and guidance. The hypocrites either fail to grasp this wisdom or imagine worldly causes, rather than God alone, control provision.
verses.8: Al-Mizan reports that the speaker was Abd Allah ibn Ubay ibn Salul, while the plural includes companions who approved and supported his words. He called himself the more honorable and the Messenger the lowlier, threatening to expel him from Medina. God reverses the claim by restricting honor to Himself, His Messenger, and believers; the hypocrites are left with humiliation and ignorance. Their failure to know this exposes the false basis of the threat.
verses.9: Al-Mizan defines al-ilhāʾ as preoccupation or engrossment and reads (63:9) as forbidding distraction by wealth and children, not possession of them. When the heart clings to these worldly adornments, it turns from remembrance of God; forgetting Him leaves only speech without deeds or heartfelt affirmation, and consequently God forgets that servant, which is manifest loss. By substituting this warning for a direct prohibition of wealth and children, the verse indicates their natural tendency to distract: believers must not cleave to them so strongly that remembrance is displaced. The prohibition is therefore figurative and, through this explicit construction, emphatic.
verses.10: Al-Mizan treats the command to spend before death as an urgent warning to believers. What God has provided is to be spent in His way before the appointed term arrives, when the dying person will ask vainly for a brief delay to give charity and become one of the righteous. The wish discloses that righteous expenditure is the needed remedy, but its time has passed. The verse therefore counters absorption in wealth, children, and worldly causes with the certainty of death and the irrevocability of the opportunity for action.
verses.11: Al-Mizan says the delay requested at death cannot be granted: when a soul's appointed term comes, God does not defer it. The fixed term is therefore no excuse for neglect beforehand, and God's complete awareness encompasses what people do in the interval given to them.
